transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-28
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Daniel Reyes (CTO, Amber Robotics), Priya Menon (ML Engineer), Sara Lopez (Infra Lead)

Auto-summary (auto): Brief notes captured by system - p95 targets around 200-300ms for short responses, 1s+ acceptable for longer summarization; concurrency up to 400 users, streaming required for interactive agents.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Samira Patel, I'm the AE on this account. Welcome.
[00:05] Daniel: Hi, Daniel here, thanks. We got Priya and Sara with me.
[00:09] Priya: Hi all.
[00:10] Liam: Hey team, Liam Chen, Redwood solutions engineer. We'll mostly cover latency/throughput, some quick notes on security.
[00:18] Sara: Cool. We're trying to get a sense of Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private — and whether we need to go on prem or can use Redwood hosted.
[00:26] Samira: Great. Could you walk through the workloads and p95 targets? That helps shape guidance.
[00:31] Daniel: Sure. Two main workloads: 1) interactive control assistant — short prompts, typically 20-80 tokens, users expect near-instant responses. We'd like p95 under 300ms if possible, 95th under 500ms is ok but we want to aim lower. 2) nightly telemetry summarization and labeling job that runs batched across many logs — longer responses, throughput oriented, p95 can be 1-2s.
[01:05] Priya: For interactive, we do streaming — users see tokens as they arrive. So streaming latency matters as much as overall completion time.
[01:12] Liam: Understood. Just to confirm concurrency — what peak concurrent users are you planning for?
[01:16] Daniel: Peak concurrency around 300-400 active sessions, bursts up to 600 for short periods.
[01:22] Samira: And tokens/sec per session roughly?
[01:25] Priya: Average session sends 30-50 tokens then 200 tokens back sometimes. So say 200 tokens returned per request on average.
[01:32] Liam: So rough tokens per second load at peak: 400 sessions * (200 tokens / few seconds) — depends on think time. But for benching we'll assume worst-case: sustained 400 concurrent requests with 200-token outputs.
[01:43] Daniel: For accuracy, we need to test both CPU-friendly quantized models and higher-precision variants; cost is a constraint.
[01:49] Samira: Right. Let's talk deployment options. Hosted gives fastest setup and easy autoscaling but less control on VPC/KMS unless you go Private. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and better isolation and you can have dedicated capacity in region X. Private is full on-prem or VPC private control plane for regulatory constraints.
[02:05] Sara: Our security team cares about KMS integration and audit logs. SOC2 is baseline; some customers require HSM-backed key wraps for keys in transit. Can Redwood integrate with our KMS?
[02:17] Liam: Yes — for Private we can do customer-managed KMS/HSM. Dedicated can also be configured with customer KMS for encryption at rest; hosted has integrations but in some cases you need Private for HSM. We have audit logs, SSO, etc.
[02:30] Daniel: Latency wise, do you have p95 numbers for the standard open Llama-ish models versus quantized variants on A100/H100?
[02:38] Liam: We have benchmarking but results vary a lot based on sequence length and batch size. For example, on H100, a 7B-13B model can hit p95 ~120-220ms for short 40-token generations at moderate batching. For 70-200 token outputs, p95 scales up — maybe 300-800ms. Quantized 4-bit runs can reduce cost but add 10-20% latency in some cases due to different kernels.
[03:03] Priya: Do you do continuous batching and KV cache reuse for multi-turn chat? We need good p95 for turn-to-turn.
[03:10] Liam: Yes, our runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache management. For multi-turn you get hit reductions and warm cache gives much lower tail latency. If you have cold starts, those are higher.
[03:18] Samira: A question — how are you measuring p95 today? In-prod telemetry?
[03:22] Daniel: We haven't pushed to prod yet for this feature. We have internal load tests using Locust and some bench scripts. We want Redwood to run a representative bench against Hosted and Dedicated to compare.
[03:32] Liam: Good — for the benchmark run we'll need 50 representative prompts, target concurrency profile, and expected p95 goals per workload. We'll instrument with token-level traces and share logs.
[03:42] Priya: We also need streaming token arrival rates — i.e., server-side token delta times — because the UX depends on first-byte and token cadence.
[03:51] Liam: We'll capture first-byte latency and token issuance rate. Can you provide sample prompts that include the longer summarization flows?
[03:58] Daniel: Yes we'll share.
[04:00] [small crosstalk]
[04:05] Sara: About Dedicated sizing — how do you recommend sizing for 400 sustained concurrent short requests? How many GPUs?
[04:12] Liam: It depends on model choice and batch sizing. Rough ballpark: for a 13B quantized model on H100-80GB with aggressive batching and continuous batching, you might serve ~100-150 concurrent short sessions per GPU with low p95. So for 400 you'd need 3-4 GPUs plus headroom. For A100 smaller throughput; you might need 5-6 A100s. We'll run sizing and give a few configs.
[04:39] Samira: And autoscaling or burst capacity options?
[04:42] Liam: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity for short spikes — you can keep minimum reserved and allow burst to shared pool or fallback to Hosted. That helps control cost while meeting peak spikes.
[04:55] Priya: On the streaming side, is there a difference between Hosted and Dedicated for token cadence?
[05:00] Liam: Network-wise, Hosted is colocated with our edge and optimized for streaming. Dedicated in customer's VPC or private cloud will have similar behavior as long as networking is stable; if you run on-prem with limited egress, you may see more variance.
[05:15] Daniel: Are there known limits on concurrent streaming connections per VM instance?
[05:19] Liam: Depends on instance type and runtime threads. We'll provide recommended connection limits per GPU node. For our baseline benchmark we'll try to saturate and observe socket and thread behavior.
[05:30] Samira: Let's capture the risk areas: cold start latency, quantization accuracy regressions, networking jitter, and throughput cliffs when KV cache invalidation occurs.
[05:41] Priya: Also tokenization differences between toy bench and prod — small token mismatches change tokens/sec math.
[05:48] Liam: Good point. We recommend running char-to-token mapping on your prompts to get accurate token counts.
[05:54] Daniel: What about cost estimates? per-token or per-hour for Dedicated?
[05:59] Samira: We'll send an indicative pricing spreadsheet. Dedicated is committed monthly/annual with GPU-hour equivalents; Hosted is usage-based per-token and can be cheaper for bursty loads. We'll include a cost-per-1000-token and a Dedicated amortized cost per GPU/hour in the spreadsheet.
[06:12] Sara: On compliance — our legal wants SOC2, ISO reports and a statement about data residency if we go Hosted.
[06:19] Liam: We can provide SOC2 report and ISO docs. Data residency: Hosted can pin regions; Private would be needed for strict residency or air-gapped.
[06:27] Daniel: For the benchmark run, how long will it take to set up?
[06:31] Liam: If using Hosted we can spin up replicas and run within 48 hours of having prompts and test plan. For Dedicated sizing on our side plus provisioning could be a week depending on region. Private takes longer due to network and KMS setup.
[06:42] Priya: Any caveats with streaming + quantization? We've seen stuttering when models stream after chunked decoding in quantized stacks.
[06:50] Liam: There can be kernel-level head-of-line delays. Our runtime does work to smooth streaming even with quantized backends, but we'll include token cadence checks in the benchmark.
[06:58] Samira: Okay let's recap next steps — Samira will send pricing, Liam will run benchmarks and propose dates, Daniel and team will share prompt set and constraints.
[07:08] Daniel: Sounds good. Quick question — competitor callouts we got: OpenAI for simplicity, Pinecone for embeddings-like retrieval — we're evaluating tradeoffs.
[07:15] Samira: Noted. We'll include notes on retrieval-augmented generation patterns and how to pair with Redwood caching.
[07:21] Priya: One more — do you support model pinning and rollout strategies? We need A/B tests.
[07:26] Liam: Yes — canary rollouts, A/B, automatic fallback to smaller models on overload. We'll include rollout docs.
[07:33] [wrap-up]
[07:35] Samira: Thanks all, we'll follow up with dates and send the spreadsheet.
[07:38] Daniel: Appreciate it, talk soon.
